cues.text: Welcome to Study Session 6 of MIT 8113, Digital Transformation and Innovation.
The title of this session is Industry 4.0, IoT and Digital Leadership.
We begin with the first chapter, the industrial revolutions.
Before we look at any technology, let us ask a simple question.
Why do we talk about revolutions in industry at all?
The answer is that, at several points in history, the way goods are made changed so deeply that businesses, workers and whole economies had to reorganise around it.
Understanding those earlier shifts helps us see what is genuinely new about Industry 4.0, and what is not.
The source gives us a table with three columns.
The first column is Revolution, the second is Major change, and the third is Enabling capability.
Let us walk through it row by row, in order.
Row one is Industry 1.0.
The major change is mechanisation.
Mechanisation means that machines take over work that people or animals did by hand.
The enabling capability is water and steam power.
In other words, it was the ability to harness water and steam as a source of energy that made machines practical for production.
Row two is Industry 2.0.
The major change is mass production.
Mass production means making large quantities of standardised goods efficiently.
The enabling capabilities are electricity and assembly lines.
Electricity gave factories a flexible and widely usable source of power, and the assembly line organised work as a sequence of steps, so that products moved along while each station did its part.
Row three is Industry 3.0.
The major change is electronic automation.
Here, machines are not only powered, they are controlled by electronics.
The enabling capabilities are computers, PLCs and IT.
PLC stands for programmable logic controller.
That is a rugged industrial computer that controls machinery by following programmed logic, for example starting a motor or stopping a conveyor when certain conditions are met.
IT, or information technology, refers to the computing and information systems that support the business.
Row four is Industry 4.0.
The major change is connected intelligent production.
The enabling capabilities are cyber-physical systems, IoT, data analytics, AI, and cloud and edge computing.
Let us unpack those terms.
A cyber-physical system is one in which physical equipment and digital computation are tightly linked, so that software monitors and influences physical processes.
IoT, the Internet of Things, means physical devices and sensors connected to networks so they can collect and exchange data.
Data analytics means examining that data to find patterns and support decisions.
AI, artificial intelligence, allows systems to learn from data and support or automate decisions.
Cloud computing offers remote, shared computing resources, while edge computing processes data close to where it is produced, such as on the factory floor.
Notice the progression.
First, power.
Then, scale.
Then, automatic control.
And now, connection and intelligence.
Now let us look at the next block, which explains what Industry 4.0 really is.
Industry 4.0 combines physical and digital systems to enable connected, data-informed and increasingly adaptive operations.
Read those three words carefully.
Connected means that machines, systems and people are linked.
Data-informed means that decisions draw on actual data from operations.
Increasingly adaptive means that operations can adjust to changing conditions, rather than running one fixed routine.
The source then makes an important warning.
Industry 4.0 is not simply replacing machines with newer machines.
Buying modern equipment alone does not make an organisation Industry 4.0.
The difference lies in integration and information, not in the age of the hardware.
The source describes smart factories.
A smart factory integrates equipment, people, software and supply chains.
The purpose is to improve quality, flexibility and responsiveness.
Quality means products that meet requirements more consistently.
Flexibility means the ability to change what, or how, you produce.
Responsiveness means reacting quickly to demand, problems or disruption.
The source then lists key design principles.
There are six, and let us take them in order.
First, interoperability.
This means that machines, devices, systems and people can communicate and work together, even when they come from different suppliers.
Second, information transparency.
This means that data from the physical world is available in digital form, giving a clear and shared view of what is happening in operations.
Third, decentralised decisions where safe.
Some decisions can be made locally, at the machine or process level, rather than waiting for a central authority.
Notice the qualification, where safe.
Decentralisation is not unlimited; it applies only where it does not create unacceptable risk.
Fourth, real-time capability.
Data is collected and acted upon quickly enough to matter for the process in question.
Fifth, modularity.
Systems are built from components that can be added, removed or reconfigured without redesigning everything.
Sixth, service orientation.
Capabilities are offered as services that can be called on and combined as needed.
To summarise this block: interoperability, information transparency, decentralised decisions where safe, real-time capability, modularity and service orientation.
Finally, the last block introduces Industry 5.0.
Industry 5.0 is an emerging complementary perspective.
It emphasises human-centricity, sustainability and resilience.
Human-centricity places people and their wellbeing, skills and creativity at the centre of technology use.
Sustainability concerns environmental and long-term responsibility.
Resilience means the ability to withstand and recover from shocks and disruption.
The source adds two careful qualifications.
First, Industry 5.0 is not a universal completed replacement for Industry 4.0.
It is complementary, and it is still emerging.
Second, we must distinguish core course content from future directions.
So for this course, Industry 4.0 is the core content, and Industry 5.0 is a perspective to be aware of, not something to treat as settled or finished.
To close this chapter: the four revolutions move from mechanisation, to mass production, to electronic automation, and then to connected intelligent production.
Industry 4.0 is about integrating physical and digital systems, guided by six design principles, while Industry 5.0 is an emerging, complementary perspective on people, sustainability and resilience.
